source.title: On the Convergence Behavior of Preconditioned Gradient Descent Toward the Rich Learning Regime
source.authors: Shuai Jiang; Alexey Voronin; E. Cyr; B. Southworth

record.tranche_reason: Tests whether grokking delays change under different optimizers and initialization scales, using accuracy trajectories on grokking tasks; it does not reproduce the original method unchanged.
record.gate_note: Rows cover reported accuracy trajectories for modular addition and MNIST, including comparisons between preconditioned and first-order optimizers. Polynomial-regression loss and Fourier-error results are not included because they do not measure the accuracy behavior named by V1 or V3. Cited results from other papers are not recorded.
record.test_reason: The study reproduces grokking on modular addition (scaled-output MLP with SGD; Power-style transformer with Adam) and on MNIST (initialization scale α). It then changes the optimizer (LM/GN/GGN versus SGD/Adam/AdamW) and measures how the train-test accuracy delay changes. This is a different method on the same question. It bears on V1, on V3 (the scale switch on non-algorithmic data) and, through grokking under plain SGD, on the adaptive-optimizer part of V7.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. The authors argue that grokking is a transition from the lazy/NTK regime to the rich regime, driven by spectral bias, and that preconditioning uniformly shortens the delay by exploring the NTK regime faster. Preconditioning alone often generalizes poorly. Switching to a first-order method restores generalization on MNIST, but on the transformer task the GGN solution is not easily continued into a generalizing one. They also argue that overfitting or adaptivity is not the main cause of grokking.
record.recipe_differences: Uses preconditioned gradient descent (LM/GN/GGN) and optimizer comparisons on grokking tasks, rather than reproducing the original training recipe unchanged; also studies MNIST and polynomial regression.
record.method_sensitivity: The delay and final generalization vary with optimizer and initialization/output scale α. In transformer modular addition, GGN produces faster validation rise but much lower final validation accuracy than Adam. In MNIST, switching from LM to AdamW recovers generalization. The cross-entropy MNIST result uses only 200 training points and is attributed to weight-norm decay.

fits_no_version.finding: On MNIST, grokking occurs whether weight norms grow, decay or stay stable, depending on the optimizer (Fig 1 top right). In cross-entropy MNIST, generalization is driven solely by weight-norm decay.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Grokking does not require decreasing weight norm, though norm decay can drive it in some settings.

record.code_released: https://github.com/sandialabs (the paper says the complete codebase will be released there after internal review)
record.problems: Main grokking trajectories are presented largely as plots without exact values or uncertainty estimates in the text. The MNIST cross-entropy result uses only 200 training points and reaches about 75%, not near-perfect accuracy. The authors note that PGD often has weaker final generalization; the delay-versus-training-set-size relationship is not tested.
record.rows_left_out: Polynomial-regression train/test loss and largest-frequency error trajectories (Figures 6 and related text) were omitted because they do not measure accuracy as named by V1 or V3. The MNIST loss-only comparison in Figure 10 was also omitted because it does not report the accuracy behavior. Additional-seed plots in Figure 13 are not separate rows because they repeat the MNIST conditions and the paper reports only minimal variation.

untested.parts: Whether the delay grows as the training set shrinks; the authors state dataset sizes are not addressed.
Text and molecule data; weight-norm interventions as a switch.
Floating-point or softmax numerical limits; adaptive-optimizer instabilities as such (it only shows grokking without adaptivity).

missing.what: LM curves for the modular-addition MLP at each α (boxed in Fig 5), described as considerably alleviating the delay
Polynomial regression: under SGD the train-test loss delay increases as α grows; LM makes the gap independent of α
Cross-entropy MNIST grokking could not be reproduced as dataset size increased
GGN→Adam continuation on the transformer needs about as many steps as plain Adam to generalize, with a validation-loss spike

record.verdict_notes: Not an original source. Most grokking evidence is figure-only, with no numeric delays. The seed robustness in Fig 13 covers MNIST only. The V7 challenge is limited to the adaptive-optimizer part; the floating-point/softmax account is untested. Selecting α to induce grokking is treated as a test of V3's scale switch, not as deliberately inducing the behaviour.

versions.untested_parts: The study tests delayed generalization on modular addition, but does not test whether the delay grows as the training set shrinks.
It does not track formation of an identifiable generalizing circuit or removal of memorizing components, nor test whether such circuit-level progress measures anticipate an accuracy jump.
Tests MNIST and initialization scaling, but not molecules or text, weight-norm changes as a switch for the delayed behavior, or a general lazy-to-rich transition across non-image settings.
No LLM pretraining or fine-tuning on realistic data.
Does not test whether low norm selects a more efficient generalizing circuit, a critical dataset size, or ungrokking below that size.
Does not identify and compare algorithms learned across runs.
Does not test adaptive-optimizer instabilities or floating-point/softmax artifacts as explanations for the delay.
